Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Visitors can hear gulls from the quay when the weather is calm; the sound is not piped into the galleries.

The chart room contains a hand-colored harbor chart dated 1912, drawn by surveyor Mina Vale for the Quay Pilot Association. A blue pencil line follows the eastern channel and ends at a small cross beside the word “shoal.” The museum’s label says the chart was used in training, but it does not identify a particular voyage or claim that the cross marks a wreck. The lower right corner is browned, and two pinholes show where the paper was once mounted. In a recording made for the museum’s opening, retired pilot Edwin Rusk said, “We learned the water by looking twice.” The chart has not been placed in direct sunlight since the museum acquired it in 2006.

At the entrance to the net loft, an iron pulley hangs above a wooden rack. The pulley is fixed in place and cannot be operated by visitors. Three bundles of netting on the rack came from different local donors between 1999 and 2017. One has large square openings and a repaired patch made with pale green cord; the donor remembered it being used for mackerel but could not give an exact date. A shorter net has tight knots and a handwritten tag reading “eel, 1964?” The question mark is part of the tag, not a museum annotation. A third bundle is made of fine brown twine, but the donor’s family did not know its original use.

The small-boat gallery presents the skiff *Morrow*, a 4.2-metre rowing boat built around 1936. Its builder is unknown. The museum bought it from the estate of Ada Pell in 1988; family correspondence says Pell used it to ferry groceries between two nearby landing points during the 1940s. No logbook survives, so the dates and frequency of those trips are not known. A narrow strip of dark paint on the inside rail is visible where most of the hull is pale gray. Conservation staff found no evidence that the strip was a formal waterline. A child’s brass button was found under a floorboard during repairs in 1991 and is displayed nearby, but there is no evidence it belonged to Pell or was originally in the boat.

The signal balcony looks over the inlet and faces a short stone breakwater. A brass hand bell on its shelf was used at the Exchange to call auction sessions to order, according to a 1903 inventory. It is not the bell tower’s original bell: the tower bell was removed before the museum opened, and its location is unknown. The balcony railing was rebuilt in 1962 after storm damage. On clear days, visitors can see the red roof of the old net-drying shed beyond the breakwater; the shed is privately owned and is not part of the museum.

The ledger room includes a book of auction entries from 1898 to 1901, open to a page recording three lots of hemp rope and a cracked brass compass. The entries list prices and buyers’ initials, not full names. Museum staff have not matched those initials to individual people. A pencilled note in the margin reads, “rain came in before noon.” The book’s cover is buckled, and the page is held open by a support rather than flattened under glass. A later account book from 1932 lists repairs to the Exchange roof, including “north drain, 14 feet” and a payment to a local mason identified only as J. Orr. The museum cannot confirm whether J. Orr is related to any current residents.

The sheltered quay is a short outdoor section behind the building. A row of iron rings is set into the stone edge, and the second ring from the stairs has a shallow notch. The museum has no record explaining how or when the notch formed. At low tide, a band of green algae is sometimes visible below the rings; the tide and light change what visitors can see. A painted white line on the paving marks the present public path, added in 2014. Older photographs show a narrower path, but the museum has no evidence that the line follows an earlier route. A bench beside the gate was donated by the Bellweather Rowing Club in 2019.

1. The route is designed for a leisurely walk and usually takes about twenty minutes, though visitors may move at their own pace. The chart room and net loft are indoors on the ground floor. The boat and ledger galleries are on the first floor and can be reached by lift or stairs. The signal balcony is accessed through the first-floor corridor; the sheltered quay is reached through the east courtyard door. The entrance desk can lend large-print transcripts. Staff ask visitors not to touch objects, lean on display cases, or cross the white line at the quay.
2. The museum’s records separate what a label documents from what a visitor might infer. Dates described as “around” or “about” are estimates. Donor recollections are attributed to donors, and uncertain writing on an object should remain visibly uncertain in any description. The boat is called *Morrow* in the collection record, but the origin of the name is not documented. The museum’s preferred wording for the auction hall’s original use is “public auction hall for fishing gear, sailcloth, and imported rope”; it was not a fish market.
3. The route can change temporarily for building access. If the gallery 3 north door remains closed on Saturday, visitors should use the east lift to reach the small-boat gallery and return by the same lift; the north door is not part of the route in that case. The building manager checks the door before each Saturday opening. The condition is current only for that day and does not mean the north door is permanently closed. The east courtyard door to the quay remains the usual exit unless staff announce otherwise.

The museum’s current audience includes local residents, school groups, and people visiting the inlet for the first time. This route is meant to connect the Exchange’s working history with the specific objects and spaces that survive, rather than tell a complete history of the harbor. The old building has had several repairs, and the collection combines documented records with objects whose previous uses are partly or wholly unknown. Avoid presenting the fictional museum as a real institution or implying that the displayed objects establish more than the notes say. The final stop is outdoors, where the view and tide vary; a visitor may see the rings and paving clearly even when the algae is hidden. The staff have asked that the audio guide end at the quay without suggesting that visitors leave the public path.
